    Publish your ontology

    Last updated on 2026-11-18 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 60 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do you prepare an ontology’s metadata and version identifiers for publication?
    • How do you assess askwol findings and check generated documentation against the ontology’s RDF?
    • How do you publish RDF and documentation using stable Web identifiers?
    • How do you check that ontology and term IRIs retrieve the intended RDF and documentation?

    Objectives

    By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

    • Prepare an ontology’s metadata and version identifiers for publication.
    • Assess askwol findings and check generated documentation against the ontology’s RDF.
    • Publish RDF and documentation using stable Web identifiers.
    • Check that ontology and term IRIs retrieve the intended RDF and documentation.

    Our research team can now use the bicycle ontology to compare inventory records. We will prepare it for publication so other researchers can inspect its definitions and reuse its terms.

    The askwol publication guide provides the reference explanations and application commands. Here, we apply that guidance to the bicycle ontology and work through one publishing route: GitHub Pages hosts the files, and w3id redirects the identifiers to them.

    This course publishes the bicycle ontology as Turtle alongside its pyLODE documentation. Both are served by the course’s GitHub Pages site. The ontology contains definitions only. It uses the https://w3id.org/bicycle-ontology/ namespace throughout the course; its w3id registration is pending. The walkthrough below shows how to prepare your own publication and configure identifier resolution.

    Public deployment in this example requires a GitHub account, permission to publish a public repository and a project identifier you intend to maintain. Replace YOUR-OWNER below with the repository owner’s GitHub username or organisation name, and YOUR-PROJECT with an available project path chosen using w3id’s naming guidance.

    Metadata and licence

    Save a copy of the complete bicycle ontology as bicycle-ontology.ttl. Its ontology header already records a title, description, creators, publisher, dates, licence and version. Use the guide’s metadata and licence sections when reviewing these values.

    Retain the original attribution and CC BY 4.0 licence for this example. If you adapt it, record your contribution and update the description and modification date to reflect your changes.

    Agree any additional project requirements before publication, and use the ontology-validation method to check their presence in the RDF. For example, a project can require an ontology title and a licence IRI. TIB’s draft metadata recommendations provide examples for ontologies and their terms.

    If you also publish research data described using your ontology, provide metadata for the dataset and its downloadable files. See the W3C’s guidance on descriptive metadata, which recommends the Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT).

    Version identifiers

    The supplied ontology records version 1.0.0 with owl:versionInfo. A separate version IRI is optional; the version-specific publication instructions show how to preserve a release at its own IRI. Use the guide’s versioning section as a reference for the OWL versioning convention.

    For your own publication, apply the IRI strategy from chapter 3: replace https://w3id.org/bicycle-ontology/ with https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/ throughout the publication copy. This updates the ontology IRI and its namespace declarations. The resulting identifiers include:

    Identifies IRI
    Ontology https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/
    Bicycle class https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/def/Bicycle
    hasComponent property https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/def/hasComponent

    The publication copy’s ontology header retains its other metadata and version information:

    <https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/> a owl:Ontology ;
    owl:versionInfo "1.0.0" .

    The owl: prefix is already declared in bicycle-ontology.ttl. Apply the same namespace replacement to the queries and shapes used to check this copy.

    Before publishing, check that the ontology and term IRIs are spelled correctly and follow your chosen IRI strategy, since users will rely on these identifiers remaining stable. Changing them later can require time-consuming updates to datasets and queries and leave users unsure which IRIs to use. See the W3C’s guidance on identifier persistence and the costs of multiple identifiers for the same resource.

    Review with askwol

    Open askwol and upload the prepared bicycle-ontology.ttl to review its contents before generating documentation. Follow the guide links beside individual findings as you review the report, and record which findings you resolve and the reasons for retaining any deliberate modelling or documentation choices.

    The reference ontology provides English and Dutch labels. A language consistency finding on a new term can identify a missing translation.

    Because askwol also checks whether namespaces resolve on the Web, a warning for your new namespace is expected until its w3id redirects are live. Investigate findings about existing external vocabularies now, and recheck your new namespace after deployment.

    Use the checks from chapter 6 to review changes that affect the model or its use. The guide describes the coverage of askwol’s reasoning checks.

    Generate and review documentation

    Local generation requires Python 3.12 or newer. Open a terminal and use cd to select the folder containing bicycle-ontology.ttl, as in the conversion setup.

    On macOS/Linux, use the environment creation and activation commands in the guide’s setup instructions. On Windows PowerShell, use:

    POWERSHELL 

    python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

    Python’s environment instructions cover activation on other shells and PowerShell execution settings. With the environment activated, install the tested pyLODE version and generate the documentation:

    SH 

    python -m pip install pylode==3.6.1
pylode bicycle-ontology.ttl -o index.html

    Open index.html in a browser. Locate Bicycle and hasComponent, and compare their displayed definitions with the RDF. Check that labels and definitions display correctly and that the licence, ontology IRI and version information agree with bicycle-ontology.ttl. Inspect advanced axioms, such as InventoryRecord’s key, in the Turtle file: pyLODE does not render every construct. After correcting the RDF, regenerate the page. Check external term links now and your new term links after publication.

    The course’s generated page shows the expected layout for the supplied ontology.

    The building walkthrough introduced labels and definitions as entity annotations. Annotations can also document the ontology, individual axioms or other annotations. An axiom annotation can record evidence for a particular subclass statement. A source or review note helps people assess the statement; adding it leaves the class memberships inferred in our example unchanged. See annotations.

    The cheat sheet gives the declaration, annotation and ontology-header patterns.

    Publish RDF and documentation

    Host the files

    1. On GitHub, create a public repository named bicycle-ontology, with a README to initialise its main branch. A repository stores the files and their change history. See GitHub’s site creation instructions.
    2. Use Add file > Upload files to upload the reviewed bicycle-ontology.ttl and generated index.html to the repository root. Commit the upload to save it.
    3. Create an empty .nojekyll file at the repository root. This tells GitHub Pages to skip its default website builder, Jekyll, and publish the HTML already generated by pyLODE. See publishing prepared files. Under Settings > Pages, select Deploy from a branch, main and /(root), then save. See publishing source.

    The repository should contain:

    .nojekyll
README.md
index.html
bicycle-ontology.ttl

    When deployment finishes, Settings > Pages > Visit site opens https://YOUR-OWNER.github.io/bicycle-ontology/. The ontology documentation should appear there. Open https://YOUR-OWNER.github.io/bicycle-ontology/bicycle-ontology.ttl too, and confirm that both files are available before requesting redirects. GitHub Pages determines content types from file extensions; its MIME type guidance explains how these are assigned.

    Connect the identifiers

    Follow w3id’s identifier creation instructions to fork its repository, creating your own copy in which to propose changes. In that copy, create ids/YOUR-PROJECT/.htaccess. This file configures the redirects on w3id. Add the following rules, replacing YOUR-NAME with the maintainer’s name and YOUR-USERNAME with their personal GitHub username. YOUR-OWNER remains the account or organisation that owns the ontology repository.

    APACHE 

    # Identifier: https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/
# Maintainer: YOUR-NAME
# GitHub username: YOUR-USERNAME

RewriteEngine On
Header always merge Vary Accept

RewriteCond %{HTTP_ACCEPT} text/turtle [NC]
RewriteRule ^(?:def(?:/[^/]*)?)?$ https://YOUR-OWNER.github.io/bicycle-ontology/bicycle-ontology.ttl [R=303,L]
RewriteRule ^(?:def(?:/[^/]*)?)?$ https://YOUR-OWNER.github.io/bicycle-ontology/ [R=303,L]

    These rules direct explicit Turtle requests to the RDF and other requests to the documentation. The ontology, namespace and term IRIs select the current files. The guide explains HTTP delivery; w3id documents the redirect rule syntax.

    To preserve version 1.0.0 at https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/1.0.0:

    1. Add owl:versionIRI to the publication copy’s existing ontology header, keeping its other metadata:

      <https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/> a owl:Ontology ;
    owl:versionIRI <https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/1.0.0> ;
    owl:versionInfo "1.0.0" .

    2. Regenerate index.html and upload both updated root files. Use Add file > Create new file to create releases/1.0.0/bicycle-ontology.ttl, pasting the reviewed Turtle into it. Create releases/1.0.0/index.html with the generated HTML in the same way. Confirm that both release URLs are available on GitHub Pages.

    3. Insert these rules before the current-file rules in your proposed w3id .htaccess:

      APACHE 

      RewriteCond %{HTTP_ACCEPT} text/turtle [NC]
RewriteRule ^1\.0\.0/?$ https://YOUR-OWNER.github.io/bicycle-ontology/releases/1.0.0/bicycle-ontology.ttl [R=303,L]
RewriteRule ^1\.0\.0/?$ https://YOUR-OWNER.github.io/bicycle-ontology/releases/1.0.0/ [R=303,L]

    The version IRI selects the preserved release; the root files provide the current publication. Keep the release files unchanged when publishing a later version. After deployment, check the version IRI with both Accept headers: expect a 303 redirect to the release’s Turtle or HTML, followed by 200 with the corresponding content type. At this first publication, the current and version-specific RDF should contain the same statements.

    Use w3id’s testing instructions before submitting a pull request, a request for the maintainers to review and merge your rules. The identifiers become available after the accepted change is deployed. The .htaccess belongs in the w3id repository; the ontology and HTML files remain on GitHub Pages.

    Check Web access

    Once the redirects are live, open the ontology IRI and Bicycle class IRI in a browser. Each should lead to the documentation. Follow term links on the page and check that you can find the corresponding definitions.

    To check RDF access, open a terminal and use curl, a command-line application for making Web requests. The command is curl on macOS/Linux and curl.exe in Windows PowerShell. If it is unavailable, follow curl’s installation guidance.

    Replace YOUR-PROJECT before running:

    SH 

    curl -L -D headers.txt -H "Accept: text/turtle" -o retrieved.ttl "https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT/def/Bicycle"

    -L follows redirects, -D saves response headers, -H requests Turtle and -o saves the response body. Open headers.txt and retrieved.ttl in a text editor. The expected responses are:

    Requested IRI Accept header Redirect destination Final response
    / text/html bicycle-ontology/ 200, text/html
    / text/turtle bicycle-ontology/bicycle-ontology.ttl 200, text/turtle
    /def/Bicycle text/turtle bicycle-ontology/bicycle-ontology.ttl 200, text/turtle
    /def/hasComponent text/turtle bicycle-ontology/bicycle-ontology.ttl 200, text/turtle

    The request paths above follow https://w3id.org/YOUR-PROJECT; destinations follow https://YOUR-OWNER.github.io/. Each listed request should first receive a 303 redirect. A final content type may include a character encoding, such as text/html; charset=utf-8.

    Repeat the command for the other paths, using Accept: text/html and -o retrieved.html for the HTML check. Load the retrieved Turtle in Protégé and confirm that it contains the expected ontology IRI, version information, Bicycle’s definition and hasComponent’s domain and range.

    Upload retrieved.ttl to askwol to review the published RDF, checking that your new namespace now resolves. If a request fails, use the recorded redirect destination to locate whether the problem is in the w3id rule or the hosted file. If you correct the RDF, regenerate its documentation and republish the affected files. Repeat the affected checks once any file or redirect corrections are deployed.

    After the checks pass, share the ontology IRI with the research community and, where suitable, submit it to a relevant vocabulary catalogue.

    Key Points

    • A publication-ready ontology file has complete metadata (title, description, creators, publisher, dates, licence) and a recorded version in its header.
    • askwol review and generated pyLODE documentation should be checked against the underlying RDF; pyLODE does not render every advanced axiom.
    • One publishing route hosts the Turtle and HTML files on GitHub Pages and uses w3id .htaccess rules to redirect stable identifiers to them, content-negotiated by Accept header.
    • A version IRI can preserve a specific release at its own stable address, alongside the current publication at the main ontology IRI.
    • After deployment, check Web access with a tool such as curl, requesting both Turtle and HTML, and confirm the expected 303 redirect followed by a 200 response.
    • Keep the IRI strategy stable before publishing: changing ontology or term IRIs afterwards is costly for everyone who has reused them.
